newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas businessmen warily urge free trade.
newsitem.headline: Americas businessmen warily urge free trade.

text.p: Businessmen from Alaska to Argentina urged their governments on Wednesday to press ahead with caution in building a hemispheric free trade area.

More than 2,000 business leaders, gathered in Brazil's third-largest city for a forum that ran parallel to talks between trade officials, gave their backing to the dream of a 34-nation Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA).
But Brazilian and U.S. businessmen disagreed on the pace at which regional trade barriers should be pulled down.

"When fully implemented, the FTAA would comprise the largest free trade arrangement in history -- bringing together nations with a combined gross domestic product of more than $9.0 trillion," an enthusiastic U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley told the Third Business Forum of the Americas.

"It would be the crowning achievement to a decade where virtually every country in the region has made progress in opening borders or providing greater access to previously closed markets," he said at the opening ceremony.

Just a short taxi ride away, deputy trade and foreign ministers were into their second day of negotiations on a ministerial declaration that will be signed by their political bosses on Friday at the Third Meeting of the Americas.
The FTAA project was born at the Miami summit in 1994, when every regional leader except Cuba's Fidel Castro agreed to set up a free trade area in the region by 2005.

The dream has since clashed with the reality of commercial interests and talks have been bogged down by a dispute between the United States and South America's Mercosur trade bloc, led by Brazil, over the speed of eventual tariff cuts.
Brazilian Foreign Ministry sources said formal free trade talks should begin after the second presidential Summit of the Americas in Santiago, Chile, next March.

But while the United States wants to discuss everything from tariff cuts to subsidies at once, Mercosur members Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and Argentina want to go step by step and leave the opening up of their economies to last.
"The FTAA cannot be set up in a rush," Brazilian Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles told reporters.
"In Brazil's case, we have made the greatest of efforts in opening up our economy. Now our industries need a period in which to adapt to the new reality," he added.
The Brazilian government position, which U.S. diplomatic sources said was beginning to grate on Washington's nerves, was being supported by Brazilian industry.
"Our position is that (the FTAA) ... must be carried out with calm, step-by-step, and above all, it must not harm Mercosur," said Luis Furlan, head of meatpackers Sadia SA.
Senator Fernando Bezerra, head of Brazil's National Industry Confederation (CNI), gave the same line, saying "balance, rythmn, realism and pragmatism" were fundamental.
Donald Fites, head of the U.S. businessmen's delegation and chairman of Caterpillar, told Brazil's Gazeta Mercantil financial daily he hoped to see "urgency" given to the matter.
He criticised the posturing of the Brazilian and U.S. governments, saying: "These agreements are too important to be left to just governments."
The businessmen held round table talks on Wednesday and will send their recommendations to the ministers on Friday.
